blocks.x: We're recording Mr. Phillips. Anthony Phillips.
Anthony Phillips. Did they call you Bill? Bill Phillips, yeah. Bill Phillips.

Bill Phillips. I'll mention the address is 1750 New Orleans. New Orleans Street and the date is May the 24th, 1961. In addition to Mr. Phillips, and this is Bill Russell, there's Ralph Collins and Harold Dagell. Okay, could you give your full name? Your given name then is Anthony. Anthony Phillips. How did you get the Bill name?

I tell you, when I was back in 1900, it must have been 1926, I joined the Ellsons and they called me Bill. Bill and he used that name, Bill and he thought Bill Phillips and that's the way it stood ever since then.
Can you tell us when you were born, your birth date exactly?
I was born March the 3rd, 1900.
1900, so you're 61 now.
Yeah, 61.
Where were you born? Right in the city here?
Yes, at 2613 Corn Island.
Right, not far from here then really?
It's about 12 blocks.
A few blocks from August South. Yeah.
Can you tell us anything about your family, if they played music as your father? My dad used to be a trumpet player.
Yeah, he named the old Tile Phillips. Oh yes.
How is your last name spelled? Is there an S on the end, Phillips? Yes, yes. Phillips.
H-I-L-L-I-P-S.
Were you in relation to the old bass player, you know Babe Phillips? No, I wasn't. Or any of the other, there's another trumpet player.

No, Joe Phillips, no, not the kid in the end. No, no, no, no. Bob Riley's his brother-in-law. My brother-in-law is Bob Riley. Poor yes. Louis Bob Riley, the one that stayed across the street here. Poor yes. Paul Bob Riley.
Yes, we know Paul, and we knew his father who died last year.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, that's right.
Can you tell us, say your father played trumpet? Yes. Which band, or did he work with any bands?
Well he didn't have no special bands. Yeah, he used to play jazz. And also he used to be an accordion player, you know. Accordion.
Did he belong to any band? Did he play brass bands or dance bands?

He played dance bands and brass bands. That was way back here. That was Ron and one Manu Parise, a young man at that time. He was playing with him then? No, I didn't play with Manu. No, he didn't play with Manu. Your daddy, your daddy. No, he didn't play with Manu. He played bowling, bowling, some bowling. Buddy bowling? Buddy bowling, some way. Yeah, that's quite a long time before.
Yeah, I guess your father's dead now, is he? Yeah, he's dead now. Remember the year he died and about how old he was then?
Well my daddy died, my daddy was 59 years old.
59, how long ago?

He died in 19... 19... 1907, 1906 or something. Oh, way back that far. Yeah. That far back. When you were just a little boy. Yeah, I was very small. I guess you never really knew him very much. You heard him. Not too good. I remember hearing him like some other. What was his name? Oktow Phillip. Oktow Phillip.
Oktow Phillip. Oktow Phillip. Oktow Phillip. Oktow Phillip.
Oktow Phillip.
Oktow Phillip.
Oktow Phillip. Oktow Phillip. Oktow Phillip.
We'll watch for the name of other people, no doubt, they'll mention it sometime. I don't remember. Maybe somebody else has already mentioned it. Oktow Phillip.
Oktow Phillip.
Oktow Phillip. Oktow Phillip. Oktow Phillip.
The bass player Gaspar is the name of that player. That's how they get the nickname, Oktow Phillip.
Yeah.
Yeah. What did he play? A cornet you say?
Yeah, a cornet. A real cornet. He had a loan about that size.
Yeah.
A real cornet. I can picture that thing. I was small but it was brass. It was brass, half of it was green.
Do you still have a picture of him?
No, my sister, one of my sisters have it. That would be wonderful. We could find that stuff and make a copy of it. I'd like to find it myself.
We could maybe make a copy of it. Yeah.
We could try to get it because he'll make a copy of it and give you one of it. Yeah.
And you can have the original back and we can all make copies from it then.
I would appreciate it. I mean they still do those old things away, you know, and they hide them and they bear them.
Very few people save those old pictures at the same time.
Yeah.
Can you tell me about any of the earliest music you remember when you were a boy? Did you remember hearing your father play at all? Can you remember?
I remember a lot of noise but what he was playing I don't know.
You don't remember much about it?
No, I don't know much about it.
I mean no more. Do you remember the earliest dance band or brass bands when you were a boy? What they sounded like and who they were? Can you remember back then?
Yeah, I remember Manuel Perez and you mean when I was playing or?
No, before you played. Before I played anything.

Before you took up any of the- Manion Perez and they had this Clover band that had been a long time ago. Cloverleaf. Cloverleaf band. That had been way back and they had, at the time they had the old Excelsior band. Old Excelsior band. Yeah, I heard of that. I never got to hear it. That was a long time ago. That was before I started with music. I used to like music because I was a music lover. I always listened. If not I'd follow the bands around, you know what I mean? Yeah. And that's how I got to like the music. But that's the old Cloverleaf band in Manuel Perez. And well as I know of, a fellow they called, Tio was in town here. He hadn't left then. He was working with a couple of the bands. Yeah. To clarinet and tenor. Yeah. And that's about as much as I can remember about that up until I got to, you know, train music.
When did you start in music? What was your first instrument?
Drums. Drums. You started right on drums. Right on drums.
How old were you about?
When I started, I was 23.
Well you didn't start when you were a little kid now.

No, I started when I was quite a man. In 23 I started. I mean I started to practice it. But when I got out playing music it was around about 25. Because I went to the old man Cantrell for music lessons and reading lessons. And then after I went to Shalini. Old man Shalini, I went to him for about a year and a half or two years. And the first I went to Shalini and I wound up with Mr. Cantrell. And that's when, after I was there about two years, close to three years with him, then I went to Dejune's Orchestra. I think that's when I met him. You come and got me. Somebody come and got me.
Yeah, but we had a band before you went with that. Oh yeah, well yeah we had the Dejohn Phillips band. And we played at the lake together. At the lake together.

Millenburg, yeah with Willis-Darrisburg. And oh we played in a lot of places. That's what you get in there. We played at the Bamel apartment. We waked out on the boat. Which was on the lake or on the river?
No, on the Madison. On the Madison and the river.

Yeah, on the lake. On the Madison you see. Yeah, perfectly. Running from the Orleans to Madisonville. And we went to several places. Tell us a little bit more about your lessons and how come you picked up drums.
Did you like that better than any other instrument I guess? Yeah, I really liked the drums.
I really liked the drums. Yeah.
What was your first set like? Did you get a whole set like?
I had a black tuxedo set. They used to call it a tuxedo. Something like this drum here.
Is it a big bass drum?

Yeah, it was a big bass drum. It was a very big bass drum. You got a big one in the back. I got a big one in the back. Oh yeah, a big 28 inch or something. Yeah, 28. This is a 14 by 22. It was one just like this. It had a single extension on it you see. It didn't have the double. It didn't make the double.
Oh yes, the one head that you could tune that.
Yeah.
It didn't have the old ropes with the...
No. It was the leather. But I did have an overhead beater though.
You didn't have the overhead.

That overhead trap you know. Yeah. And I had kept that so long until when I went to Chicago. I don't know what happened. I went down. I went to Chicago and I left out of Chicago. I went to Springfield and I missed the place. I never could find it when I got back to Chicago you see. But that's what I had. The old tuxedo drum. Flag drum like that. Then I got a set of Puerl drum. When I went to Chicago. Peacock Puerl. I had about 15 sets I reckon all together. I got about five sets around here now. I always did like a lot of drums. That's nice.
If you like an instrument.
I keep a lot of instrument. Yeah.
You know what he do? When he come from playing a job at night before he go to bed.
Oh yeah.
He open them drums in the front room and clean them spotless. Then he go to bed.

Clean my drum. I take my bed and then I go to bed. I'm going to put them on bed. And I just keep them all in good condition. For the person to come for me to play that. It's all hooked up. That's my parade drum back there. That's a little bit of one back there. Right in the back of the door.
Yeah.
That's the little one back here. Yeah.
That's my parade drum. It's all right. It isn't so heavy to carry. Oh it's light. It's very light. Yeah. You got the simulac?
Oh yeah. It's all hooked up.
That's a little light.
Yeah. You really got that in fine shape.
Look at that nice beater and all. Look at the simulac thing.
Yeah.
Look at that.
That's the way to keep the drums. Did you make that? No. I made my beads myself. Oh you make these simul beaders. Yes. I made them myself.
Yeah. Looks like it's chromium plated.
It's shining. Yeah. It's very strong. And he come planting for red. Before you take bad heat or anything, them drums is clean. Yeah. It's better light but they have it too.
It's like a nice, nice, nice, perfect simulac. Yeah. Nice and jigging. Yeah.
That's fine. It's certainly better than most of the bands. Good sound. Good sound. Yeah. That's a real simulac. God. It's how you need to do that.

You know, somebody's been complaining about the simulac. on the Eureka band made a record and that old simulac there is about a $2 simul. It's not a ton. It couldn't be worth more than $2. No tone. It sounds like a... It doesn't sound as good as a tin lid. It sounds like a graveyard symbol. Yeah, it's awful. But that's the way it happens. Oh yeah, you've been having it coming.
Oh yeah, when I sit on that team. Yeah. You better beat it Sunday cause they'll be out there. Well, I'll be well. I'll be well. Yeah. Yeah. I'll be well. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Most of them I'll be playing with Howard, I'll play fumes over the river. I've got four parades coming up now right on the stretch.
Four?
Oh yeah, I've got Sunday morning, I've got Sunday day, I've got Monday and the 17th, huh? Yeah.

The 17th. Is it Monday or Tuesday? Oh the 17th, that's next month. Tuesday. Tuesday. Memorial Day we go. With Casimir down there. Yeah, with Casimir. The Quban down to Chalmette. That soldier's grave.
By the way, Casimir called me and told me he was going to shoot me regularly. He ain't going to fool with Knox no more.
Well Knox, do you want to pay his union?

He don't want to pay union cards. Yeah, I joined the band, I told him, it's alright with me, if they want me, it's alright with me. I've been waiting in his place, you know, all the time he's going to play the fumes. Didn't want to get no cards, but I mean you can't wait without having no cards. I keep my cards paid about a year.
What time is that Tuesday down in Chalmette?
I think it's one o'clock. One o'clock. One o'clock. One o'clock. One o'clock.
One o'clock. One o'clock. What kind of drum do you use Bill? What big drum?
Well I got a, that's a lead today. That's a lead.
The parade drum is a lead.
Yeah.
How big is that, about 24?
That's a, that's a, twelve by twenty. Twenty is all?
Twelve by twenty.
Yeah, I guess it's smaller than that. This is twelve, this is a, this is a, this is a, fourteen by twenty-two.
Twenty-two, that one looks like the diameter might be just as big. No, it's, it's, it's a, it's a, a plenty smaller.

Smaller than that. My gold drum back the bed is smaller than that. I think it's a, fourteen by eighteen. Yeah, this is a, a plenty smaller. Yeah, I guess it is. Yeah, when you get looking at it, yeah, it's, a little smaller you see. Oh yeah, it's, yeah, if that other's twenty-two then it's twenty, but it looks bigger. Yeah. That's a, this is a twelve by twenty. What size is your cymbal there? This cymbal is a ten inch.
But I have some big cymbals, I got some cymbals in there. Big old cymbals in there. Oh yeah, if that other is 22 then that's 20 but it looks bigger.
Yeah, this is a 12 by 20. What size is your symbol there? This symbol is a 10 inch. But I have some big symbols. I got some symbols there. Big old symbols. I got about 140.
That looks bigger than 10 inches.

It's about 10 or 12 inches. It must be bigger, yeah. It's about as big as a 12 inch. Yeah, it's about 12 inches. More like 12. But I have some 18 inch, 20 inch symbols. I got a lot of symbols. I got a lot of stuff on that zipper over there. I have a lot of symbols.
It's nice to have a good drum set and take care of it.
Oh yeah, you have to have a good instrument to play with.
Yeah, I think so too.
You got to have a good one. When you come to music, if you like music, you got to have something to get something. If you don't have nothing, you can't get nothing.
I wonder if you could describe, as far as how that overhead track worked. Yeah.
I can remember that.
I don't suppose you ever saved one of those, did you? Or do you know anything?

Yeah, you see I was in Chicago with Herbert Moran. You might have heard of him, Herbert Moran. Yeah, sure. I was working with him at the trumpet player. Yeah. And he had a place down at 35th and South Park. And I used to go down there and help him teach drum lessons to the drummers, you know. And my traps, I left from there. When we left from Chicago, we went to Springfield. We stood down there, I think it was about three months and a half.
And you had one of those overhead then?

I had it then. You see, I used to use it in the studio. And when I come back, there's a fella called Sandsbury, was running it while we left there. And when I come back and look for the overhead trap, I don't know if one of the guys got it out there or what. But I asked Tubby Hall, you might remember? I knew Tubby, yeah. I knew Tubby Hall, and the zoo that used to be down at the place often because we used to have our little portals down here. So I asked Tubby, I said, Tubby, I said, you ever seen my overhead trap? He said, Bill, I seen that thing. He said, well, what happened? I don't know. He said, I don't know if Santa did ever let one of the guys get away with it or what. But that's what happened. I've never even seen one of them. I don't know. Well, I tell you, it's a long rod with the bead on it, you see. And it hooks up in front here. Up on top of the drum. On the top of the drum. And the long rod would hook in the back, you see. And the spring would run from here, the back there, you see. And would keep that pedal on the swing. What kind of spring? Like a door? A screen door? It's like a screen door. Yeah. You see, when the spring would be up, it would be hooked on here. It would pull the pedal. It would set out like that, you see. Then you had a beater with a strap hooked on the bottom of the drum here. And when I would make the pedal set up, and when you hit it like that, that's when it would go down. But the spring here would pull it back. What pulled it down?
What pulled the strap?
The strap with the flow bead on it.
The strap was fastened to the beater itself?

To the beater itself. Down near your toes there then. It was hooked on there. And when you kick it down, the spring here would be holding cocked back like that. When you beat down, you see, the beater would hit here.
The strap pulls it in.
That's right.
It would pull it in. You'd raise your foot up and the spring pulls it back out.

That's right. It was something very fast. It was very fast. Fast, huh? Oh, yeah. It was fast. It was faster than beater they got. Now, that thing was very fast. Really? I never thought. Oh, yeah. You had to have a good steady foot to control it, because that thing would pull you out of time. You'd have to know what you're doing to fool the overhead trap. It really was tricky. Yeah, it was very fast. I never could buy any more. I went around around these pawnshouts and tried to, you know, like by Big Jake or Fings and tried to pick up on one, but I never could find them. Now, Black Benny had one of those same traps himself. Black Benny the drummer, you might have heard of him. Yeah, we've all heard of him. Yeah.
Bass drummer in the grids.
Yeah, yeah. He was a good drummer. He was a good man. He was a good man to have him in the band. And that's the only one I ever knew to have one of them.
How was that strap fastened to the beater itself? Did it go around the mall? No.
They had a, they had a, in the back of the ball, you see, they had a little hook, you see, and this foot pedal here would come up, you see, that strap would come up and hook that beater, you see.
In front of the beater or in back of the beater?
In the back of the beater. In the back of the beater. You see, when you go down, that would make it hit the bass drum, you see, and the spring would pull it back.
Yeah.
You understand what I mean? Yeah, I understand. And the foot pedal was made out of wood.
Oh, it's wood.
Yeah. It was wood, you see. And it screwed on the drum.
Did the foot pedal have a spring underneath it, or was it all worked from that one spring?

No, it worked from that one spring. You see, the spring here, with the hook here, and the beater, you hook the beater here, it would be straight up, and then you hook that other piece right back here, and bring that spring over, where I would cock the beater out. Uh-huh. And to get the beater here, when you take that strap, was on the, on the wooden pedal, you hook on there, and when you hit down, it would hit the bass drum.
The thing would go up like this, wouldn't you?
Yeah, yeah, yeah, I understand. You're trying to pull the pedal up? Yeah, the spring here would pull it back.
Now, when you put your drums away, did you have to disassemble all that?

No, you had to do on hook the spring, you see. I had to hook the spring, you see. In other words, relax it. Yeah. Instead of kicking up, this on hook, it would stay down, and you would just take that block, that wooden block, you didn't even put it in your case. You take that wooden block, and you'd wrap it up, and you'd put it right on the drum. You'd take your strap, and when you're holding the drum, keep it from sliding away from the chair, and you'd just wrap it around it.
Do you remember what make it was? Who made it?

It was the Slingerland. A Slingerland? Yeah, it was the Slingerland. Yeah, it was the Slingerland. It was the old make. It was the Slingerland. But that thing was beautiful. And I kept it just like new. Them guys just took it. I never could find out where it went. Never could find out. I was with Lee Collins one night, and he told me he seen a cat down at 31st Estate. That's where the Union Hall was at in Chicago, you know? Oh yeah. You see a fella with a trap wrapped up, but he didn't know if it was his or not. I said, I'd like to see him, because I had some files grooved in on that rod. I filed it, you know, in the back. I filed three little grooves in the back of it. Because if I'd have found him with it, I should have got him. Got him, got my beater from him. You better believe it. And them guys, they go around to pick up on those kind of things. You never see them no more.
That's the same.

It was really number one, very fun. You never have to change the rod or nothing. It's the middle of the ball you have to change. A lighter ball or a bigger ball. Always kept the two ball beaters, you know? You could take them off. You ain't put them off, you see?
What do you keep two for a spare?

Yeah, you keep one for a spare. Sometimes you get on an open job where you put that heartbeat on you. You get a bigger tone out of it, you see? A louder tone, you see? In the open air. In the open air, yeah. You play, you have a lot of tone, you see?
When you, I guess you had to get a foot, sort of, what do you call these things now? Beat them?
Beat them.
Yeah, you had to get one of these, not the overhead, but underneath after that, did you?
Well, when the beat, after I lost the beatle, well I had to get the regular beatle. The regular beatle?
Yeah, the regular beatle beatle. Now, did you have any trouble then?
What?
When you switched?
No, I didn't have any trouble.
It worked alright.

It was just a little slow, but it worked alright, you see? You had more knee, you had more ankle action than anything else, because I had been used to that, you know, that overhead and it was faster, but most of the time you had to push that thing back and forth. Of course the traps, at that time, it ain't like the traps today. The traps are much faster than they do, you see? They were slow, you see? But at that time the traps were much slower, the springs was weaker or something, I don't know what it was, but today they're very, they're plenty faster.
They make them ball bearing and water and fire.

Yeah, yeah, they're very fast, they're very fast today. There's a lot of difference, and then they're not, you see? There's something, you got to do it. Even you take the fumes, long years ago, I was playing fumes with Chris Kelly and Buddy and then they got the fumes more since the day, you play, you play, four beats still measure, but at that time you hit that bass, 12 hit one, and the stage on the four, three. The generator. That's the many players today, you see? Long years ago, they got one beat on that bass too. One, two, three, four.
Yeah, one, two, three, four. Why do you think they changed the style like that?
No, the style ain't changed, it's just a question they don't want to get under much quicker. They want to what?
They get under much quicker. They want to march a little faster.
That's right, a little faster.
A little faster.

A little faster. A little faster. A little faster. It won't take much time. It won't take much time. You take the snare drum player, and the minute they stop playing the fumes, you pick up one at a time. Then you get to the graveyard faster, because if you wouldn't do that, you'd be all, you'd need about one o'clock, it'd be nine o'clock at night before you get to the graveyard or something like that. I mean, it'd take you much longer, you know what I mean? So I mean that way they'd rush it on. In other words, you walk faster now? Yeah, well you walk faster. In the fumes you walk, yeah you walk a little bit faster, not too much faster, but you walk a little faster at them times, you know what I mean? And you take also in the street parading. If you can a parade down, you take like up there on Cornwall there from the Lions Club by the way, if you bass drum player and you know how to pick up on the time, you'd be all day long getting down there. You'd be two o'clock and you still wouldn't be the Canal Street. So you have to pick them up and care them while they're fresh, while they got that good walking spirit about them, you see? Well you can linger coming back. You want to get them down there the whole walk while you're fresh. Because if you linger along while you're fresh, when you're coming back, you're going to have to drag you back. So you got to bring them down there and bring yourself too while you're fresh. And then coming back, you know what I mean? You can take it easy. And then as you get after two o'clock you want to try to step them up again because the time is getting short. The 60 some odd blocks from the den, you try to get them back there before you get too tired, you see? Then them guys there start getting tired too and then they're full of juice and full of fun. Well they started slowing up too, you see? So the bands slow up and they're slow but by your, just keep them on going, you understand? They'll keep them on moving, they be moving, they be tired but they be still moving. Because if you don't do that, you're going to be running late. Last year we used to knock off at 6 o'clock. Last year at 5.30 we was done. I mean, I mean, guys was done, they had their fun, they was tired and it was a good thing we got them back because they kind of burned out their stuff. They didn't care about going no more, that was there no. When we got in the den that was it. They paid off and then for five minutes after six I was home. Which parade was that? The Lions Club. The Lions Club. I've been waiting up there for them for about six or seven years. They have a pretty good club, nice fellas to get along with. And they have two bands. You see, if you work with one band on the parade on the corner of the day, it might be a shorter run to further than you're going to know you play the parade with one band. You don't have no rest because every time you stop everybody has music, everywhere you pass. Music. You might just stop playing and you don't know whether you want to hear music. When you got two bands you relax for maybe three or four blocks or at least three blocks and the other band will give you a little relaxation, you understand? When you got that one band proposition, no sooner you stop you don't walk a block. Fellas are out of music and the snare drum player he's going to catch some sand because I do stop. But when he start he don't stop. When he, with that five minutes of whistle, seven minutes whistle blowing in the morning on the corner of the morning, he don't stop no more, that's him. Yeah, that's right. You got to beat the time because they want that more, boom. Them fellas want to march by that, you see? Well I'm relaxing, I'm walking for a couple of blocks of that bass drum on my shoulder, you see? But he don't have no rest. That's the end of him. That's one reason I got away from playing snare drum. A lot of fellas ask me not to play snare drum. I don't want to play no snare drum. I'd rather play the bass drum. Man, you'd rather have that bass drum. I say I got a light drum to catch, don't worry about it. Even though I have that thing on my shoulder every time. You understand? I do get a rest. But the guy with the snare drum, he don't get the motor. That's all. When you knock off, that's all he is.
I wish y'all could have seen little Jim playing the parades. He had a big, big drum up like that. Then you couldn't see him back up. You couldn't see him with the bass.
He had to look as he was behind the bass. And he played them parades too. Oh yeah, Jim played a many parades. He's in the Cross the River.
Yeah.

Yeah, yeah. He played a many parades. He played a lot of music. It's a wonderful thing. I just like music. I don't know how I just like music. It's one of those kind of things. When you like something, you want to stop. My wife tell me all the time, old man, you're getting old. I say, it looks like the older I get, the better I feel. You know. Good that you like music. I really like music. The first year out of the hospital, I asked Dr. Preacher. I said, Doc, I said, we all right to walk a parade? I put the bass drum across my back. He said, Philip, how long you gonna walk? I said, about seven, eight hours. He said, if you can walk for about three, four straight months, you can make out better. You need to tell those stories. Because I come out, I was bent over like that, man. I was straight as a picket. He said, the more you walk, the better it is for you. So my wife, she was kind of scared. And I had to take her up there to the doctor, let her, the doctor tell her that it was all right for me to play the bass drum again. Oh, well she satisfied me. I really like to play bass drum. I just like music. It's crazy about music. I remember one time, it was there in 1922 St. Peter Street, we used to rehearse at least five or six times a week. Oh yeah. Oh yeah, five or six times a week.
And have three or four watermelons. Three or four watermelons. Pot of red, beat the rice. He used to wake in a watermelon. The fruit business. That's what I do now.
I'm still in the fruit business. I peddle, you see. Yeah. Yeah, I have my truck out there. Big, minor red beans, rice.
Big, red beans, rice.

Always did have a large house. Just me and my wife, all my kids is gone. Plenty of company on, plenty of room. I got a whole trunk of music out there. We bought more music and then the two bands sit on there. Harry and I, these brothers, the old days, I love, we bought some music. Just buy music. Everything late come out, he'd come with a stack. Leo, he'd come with a stack. I'd get down and sometimes he'd have three, four copies of the same number.
We used to join these different music clubs, you see. Yeah. And every number come out. Sometimes three music clubs will send you the same number, you know what I mean? As they come out to me.
I got a whole trunk of Raymond out there from Louis Armstrong, bought some Walter Pesaw made. I just like music. I keep all that stuff so straight. That's good to keep it. You never tell.
It's valuable sometimes. Oh yeah.
It's very, very, very handy.
Well, all I think of it, did you have any brothers that played any instrument? Anybody else in the family besides your father that ever played music?
Nobody but my father. No uncles or anyone either?
No, no.
I got all my in-laws, a lot of them. Richard McLean, he married my niece, Beatrice, who died there. She died about a couple of months ago. Oh yes, I remember that.
Yeah, Richard McLean.
Richard McLean, Louis Barber, T-Boy Barber, and Lucy, one of these days.
Richard used to play banjo with Kid Rene.
Yeah, with Kid Rene. He played bass now.
Yeah.
And we interviewed him.
He still has his banjo, nice. Yeah, yeah. He's a nice banjo. He's pretty nice musician. The mute on, has a special mute.
Yeah, yeah, he's a nice fella.
A lot of the banjo players have the mute, you know, the mute on the side. Some of them have somebody just could push it down his leg.

Yeah, use it on their knee, you know. That's his knee some of them. Yeah, some of them have that knee action on us, you know. And I like any instrument. I mean, I like a loud drum on a parade in spots. Sometimes you're playing in funerals, a lot of spots you have piano, you've got to get very soft. But I never did like no loud drum, but I like to be very active behind my drum. And now that is. Mr. F, you see me by the set of drums, you say, I can't be that old man. I don't double stage still, I sit on them springs, then. It keeps me bouncing. See that spring?
Oh yeah.

I just keep them moving all the time. And I put a hand in with sticks in my hand, you know, twisting sticks. I just, my daughter, I tell him, I say, oh man, you're all the staff. I say, I like it because you walk in the middle. I say, you like something. I say, you like something.
I say, you know, a drummer, you don't care too much of the tennis to him. You couldn't twist the sticks a little bit, you know. Oh yeah. Oh yeah, you had to twist the sticks a little bit.
Well, I think I would too. What about Tubby Hall? I used to hear him about 1938 or 39, but I never did talk to him very much. I went to his home once. Sean Heversett Brownson.
Yeah.
He interviewed his brother a couple years ago. He died, you know, minor. Yeah, yeah, minor died.
What'd they call him?

Wait a minute. Oh. I can't think now. Ram. Ram. Ram. Very nice. I asked him a little bit about his brother, but he didn't tell us very much either. Can you tell us anything about his style of playing much?

Well, I don't know. I never pay too much attention. I seen him a lot of time down by the, um, um, place. No, uh, no, not in the Union Hall. I seen him a lot of time. He was sitting with Earl Hynden and they was waking on South Park about, uh, it was 39th in South Park. Grand Terrence. Grand Terrence. I seen him a lot of time down there waking up. You know, them fellas, you look at him, you're out having fun, you didn't come from playing, you ain't even stunned by him. You didn't have Joe nice waking up. Yeah, that's right. The army sounded pretty good to me, but his style of playing and what position he's sitting on, I knew, I never knew.
I never paid too much attention. He was playing with Johnny Dodds and Natty Dominique and I, I was paying more attention to Johnny Dodds the clarinetist then and didn't know a minor hall.
Yeah, he was a nice drummer, he was a good man.
Yeah. I remember Baby Dodds, he was a good drummer. Did you ever hear Baby Dodds around Chicago or down there?

No, I never, I never heard them play because you know you get busy around there and you play it at night and you see them places you go to wake up 11, 30 at night and it's 3 or 4 in the morning and you get under you, you stop and get a drink or something, well that's usual, you know what I mean? This is going to stop somewhere. We used to stop 5th to 1st in South Park at the drugstore, they sell liquor and everything down there, you know. They get all the taste and sometimes you stop in them places and be running later, some of the fellas go awake at 12 and wait till 5 or 6 o'clock in the morning, you stop in the gym. But you all beat out, you take a few drinks, well you don't play enough music, you ain't study them out there and you meet them in places, you know what I mean? Yeah. Talking, we don't want to party, but most of the time when they playing, you playing, you never get a chance to yell unless they start early.

Anyway, I was going to say Baby Dodds told me once that he learned his press roll partly from Tubby. Yeah, yeah. I'm surprised to hear that, but I never paid much attention to Tubby. Do you remember any press roll that he did?

He could roll, he put them in the middle of the old man Cantrell. Really? He had a tough roll. He made that even, you know, and sound like Tubby man. He had two good wrists. He was tight on the wrist. He was tight on the wrist. And he never would choke his stick that, I mean just like he would choke, try to choke somebody. He let his sticks loose, you know. Just let them go for themselves, because when you test that skin, you got some good skin on that stick, that stick will knock it down if you don't hold it. And all he would do is guard it, but he had two good wrists. He had a good wrist. And a good ankle, I can tell you, he had plenty of ankle. He had a very good ankle. And that's what you need, any way you play this drum, you need a good ankle and you need a good wrist. Two good wristes, you see. And if you take care of them, saying whether you use them or not, always keep your wrist rubbed with alcohol. I'm always rubbing, every evening when I take a bed, I rub down with alcohol, because you got to keep yourself in action, you see. A lot of guys walk a corner for parade, and when they get in the parade, they're all bamboo Thank you.
I would have said she was too tight for you, then you can't do nothing.
Mr. Tubby was fat in those days, when I knew him he was pretty heavy.
Yeah he was fat, yeah Tubby. He was fat then too. You know where he got that name from Tubby Hall, he was a Tom Tom man.
No I never did know him.
No he got it from Tom Tom, he was a Tom Tom man.

segments.title: Opening: recording details and how Anthony became 'Bill'
segments.summary: Recording date and address are stated and the people present named. Phillips says he got the name Bill when he joined a band in 1926.

segments.title: Birth in 1900 and where he grew up
segments.summary: Born March 3, 1900, in New Orleans about twelve blocks from the interview site.

segments.title: Family name spelling and relatives; brother-in-law Bob Riley
segments.summary: Phillips says his father played trumpet, confirms spelling, denies kinship with other Phillips musicians, and mentions his brother-in-law.

segments.title: His father's playing and early death
segments.summary: His father played jazz, dance and brass bands, and accordion, and died about 1906-07 when Bill was small. The name of the father is discussed.

segments.title: Father's cornet and the family photograph
segments.summary: Phillips recalls his father's brass cornet and says a sister has a photograph the interviewers hope to copy.

segments.title: Bands he heard before playing: Manuel Perez, Cloverleaf, Excelsior
segments.summary: He remembers little of his father's playing but recalls following the Manuel Perez, Cloverleaf and Excelsior bands and Tio working in town.

segments.title: Starting on drums at 23, lessons and early bands
segments.summary: He started drums at 23, studied with Cantrell and Chaligny, then joined Dejan's orchestra; the interviewer recalls lake and boat jobs together.

segments.title: His first drum set and the overhead beater
segments.summary: He liked drums best; his first was a tuxedo set with a large bass drum and an overhead beater, which he kept until Chicago.

segments.title: Keeping his drums spotless; parade drum and cymbals
segments.summary: Phillips keeps many sets and cleans them after jobs. The group admires his parade drum and hand-made beaters.

segments.title: Eureka band record, upcoming parades and union cards
segments.summary: He complains of a poor cymbal on a Eureka record, lists coming parades including Memorial Day at Chalmette, and discusses Casimir and Knox and union cards.

segments.title: Sizes of his bass drums and cymbals
segments.summary: He compares drum and cymbal sizes in the room and says a drummer needs good instruments.

segments.title: Losing his overhead trap in Chicago
segments.summary: In Chicago he worked with Herbert Moran, helped teach drummers, then left for Springfield and lost his overhead trap; Tubby Hall could not help find it.

segments.title: How the overhead trap worked; Black Benny
segments.summary: He describes the spring, strap and beater mechanism in detail, says it was very fast, and names Black Benny as the only other drummer with one.

segments.title: Mechanism details, the Slingerland make, and the stolen trap
segments.summary: He answers questions on the strap, wooden pedal and packing of the overhead trap, names Slingerland as maker, and tells how it was stolen.

segments.title: Spare beaters and switching to the regular pedal
segments.summary: He explains keeping spare beater balls and says the regular pedal was slower than the overhead one but worked.

segments.title: Funeral and parade tempo and the bass drummer's pacing
segments.summary: He explains how beats and walking pace changed at funerals, how a bass drummer paces a long Lions Club parade, and why he prefers bass to snare.

segments.chapter: Music as a way of life
segments.title: Little Jim's parade playing and returning to parades after hospital
segments.summary: Remarks on a big-drum player, then his doctor lets him march again with the bass drum after illness.

segments.chapter: Music as a way of life
segments.title: Rehearsals, fruit business and his music collection
segments.summary: He recalls rehearsing in 1922, says he now peddles fruit, and shows a trunk of sheet music he kept.

segments.chapter: Music as a way of life
segments.title: In-laws: Richard McLean and the Barbarins; loud drums and active playing
segments.summary: No other relatives played music except in-laws such as Richard McLean, who played with Kid Rena. He says he likes to stay active behind the drums.

segments.chapter: Music as a way of life
segments.title: Twisting sticks and bouncing on the drum stool
segments.summary: He describes keeping the drum springs bouncing and twisting his sticks.

segments.title: Tubby Hall and Minor Hall in Chicago
segments.summary: Asked about Tubby Hall, he recalls seeing Minor Hall in Chicago and says he never heard Baby Dodds because of late-night work.

segments.title: Tubby Hall's press roll, wrists, and nickname
segments.summary: Phillips praises Tubby Hall's wrists, ankles and roll, advises care of the wrists, and says Hall's nickname came from being a Tom Tom man.
